stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Built from rare purple Cambrian sandstone, magnificent St. Davids Cathedral enshrines St. David’s restored medieval shrine—still drawing pilgrims from every corner of Britain.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: In Welsh, his famous last words read "Gwnewch y pethau bychain"—"Do the little things"—a spiritual gem echoed centuries later by St. Thérèse of Lisieux!
stops.saintQuote: Be joyful, keep the faith, and do the little things you have heard and seen me do.

completionSummary: You walked the Gothic spires of medieval Prague with Princess St. Agnes of Bohemia—who turned down kings and emperors to correspond with St. Clare of Assisi, build Prague’s great hospital for the poor, and inspire Czechoslovakia’s peaceful Velvet Revolution.

stops.title: The Princess Who Turned Down an Emperor
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Hradčany (Prague Castle) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Golden sunlit spires of medieval Prague Castle perched high above the curving Vltava River.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: St. Agnes of Bohemia stands revered as one of the supreme patron saints of the Czech Republic.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Emperor Frederick II was surprisingly gracious when Princess Agnes turned him down, famously remarking: "If she had left me for a mortal man I would have taken vengeance with the sword—but I cannot take offense because she preferred the King of Heaven to me!"
stops.saintQuote: I prefer the poverty of Christ to all the empires of this world.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Born daughter of King Ottokar I of Bohemia and Queen Constance of Hungary—first cousin to St. Elizabeth of Hungary—young Princess Agnes was sought in marriage by King Henry III of England AND Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II! Astonishing Europe, she wrote straight to Pope Gregory IX asking to refuse all earthly thrones so she could wed Christ in radical Franciscan poverty.

stops.title: Letters with St. Clare at Agnes’s Convent
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Convent of St. Agnes to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: 1234 – 1282 AD · First Poor Clares North of the Alps
stops.imageCaption: Soaring early Gothic vaulted brick-and-stone cloister of St. Agnes Convent in Prague bathed in crisp golden winter light.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today the stunningly restored Convent of St. Agnes of Bohemia houses the Czech National Gallery’s medieval sacred art collection.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: An ancient 700-year-old Bohemian prophecy foretold: "When Agnes is finally canonized, Bohemia will be free!" Pope John Paul II canonized St. Agnes of Bohemia on November 12, 1989—and FIVE DAYS LATER, Czechoslovakia’s peaceful Velvet Revolution began, toppling Communism without a single shot fired!
stops.saintQuote: Hold fast to poverty, humility, and joyful charity.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: Find the luminous focal point of Convent of St. Agnes in the scene.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Scan the center-left horizon of the painting.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Letters with St. Clare at Agnes’s Convent
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Entering the brand-new Poor Clare monastery she built in Prague—the very first north of the Alps—Agnes forged a legendary lifelong pen-pal friendship with St. Clare of Assisi. Clare’s four surviving letters to Agnes ("my other half") are among the greatest spiritual treasures of the Middle Ages. For nearly fifty years, the former princess mended lepers’ clothes, cooked meals, and comforted Prague during famine and war.

completionSummary: You walked the astonishing philanthropic and missionary trail of St. Katharine Drexel—the Philadelphia heiress who gave away her $20 million inheritance to build over 60 schools and Xavier University of Louisiana for Native American and Black communities.

stops.title: The Heiress Who Opened Her Mansion to the Poor
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Walnut Street & Torresdale to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: 19th-century red-brick Philadelphia townhouse doorway where baskets of food and warm wool coats are handed gently to waiting families.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: St. Katharine Drexel’s tomb rests inside Philadelphia’s majestic Cathedral Basilica of Sts. Peter and Paul, drawing pilgrims honoring her lifelong stand against racial injustice.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When her father died in 1885, Katharine and her two sisters inherited a $14 million trust—worth roughly $400 million in today’s money—earning her over $1,000 a day in 1880s dollars!
stops.saintQuote: If we wish to serve God and love our neighbor well, we must manifest our joy in the service we render.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Appointed Archbishop of San Salvador in 1977, Romero chose to live not in an episcopal mansion but in a tiny three-room cottage on the grounds of a charitable cancer hospital. globeHeaderSubtitle: Sacred Trails of St. Anthony Mary Claret (Sallent, Vic, Santiago de Cuba & Fontfroide)
completionSummary: You crossed Catalonia and the Caribbean with St. Anthony Mary Claret—the weaver’s son who walked thousands of miles preaching on foot, founded the Claretian Missionaries, championed justice for enslaved people in Cuba, and printed millions of accessible books.

stops.title: The Weaver’s Loom in Sallent
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Sallent de Llobregat to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm sunlight streaming through a nineteenth-century Catalan textile workshop with wooden weaving looms and golden spools of thread.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Claret’s family home in Sallent has been lovingly preserved as a museum showing the weaver’s workshop where his practical, hardworking spirit was shaped.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Anthony never lost his practical inventor’s mind—later in Cuba he even wrote helpful manuals on sustainable agriculture and started low-interest credit unions for poor farmers!
stops.saintQuote: The love of Christ urges us on—we cannot stay silent.

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Santiago de Cuba to uncover 3 hidden memories

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When a would-be assassin slashed Claret’s face with a razor in Holguín in 1856, the wounded Archbishop personally begged the governor to spare the attacker’s life!

stops.title: Peaceful Exile at Fontfroide Abbey
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Abbaye de Fontfroide to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Serene golden-limestone Cistercian abbey cloister framed by blooming rose gardens and sun-warmed Mediterranean cypress hills.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: The rose-filled golden cloisters of Fontfroide Abbey preserve the serene chamber where the tireless missionary finally laid down his walking staff.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Pope Pius XII canonized St. Anthony Mary Claret in 1950, and today Claretian missionaries serve in over seventy countries across six continents!

Welcomed warmly by Cistercian monks at Fontfroide Abbey in southern France, he passed peacefully to God on October 24, 1870.
